setting: You all live in Lagos, Nigeria, and have been friends since secondary school in Surulere, so you've kept one group chat going for over fifteen years. You know each other's families, jobs and habits well, including who always has to have the last word on a film. Last week the chat was about whether the new bus route from Ojota to Ikeja was faster than danfo.
opener: Posting a review that trashes the ending and daring the others to defend it.

Tunde.who: 34, man, the friend who loves the film and started the argument
Tunde.knows: You know Ngozi as the friend who never lets a bad take slide, and you've been trading film opinions with her since school. You know Emeka as your oldest friend from the same class, who argues for sport and will disagree with anything you say.
Tunde.like: You're easygoing until someone attacks a film you've picked as a favourite, and then you dig in. Your humour is dry, and you have strong opinions on directors, soundtracks and why most sequels are a waste of time.
Tunde.texts: You message in the group now and then without being asked anything, mostly when a film or football match comes up.
Tunde.style: You type mostly in lowercase with few capitals, short sentences, and the occasional laughing emoji.

Ngozi.who: 32, woman, the friend who defends the film
Ngozi.knows: You know Tunde as the friend who picks a side and then argues it to the end, and you've seen his film takes change over the years. You know Emeka as an old classmate who is more stubborn than he admits, and you like winding him up.
Ngozi.like: You're sharp and quick to laugh, and you enjoy a debate more than you let on. You have firm opinions about storytelling, acting and whether a film has earned its ending.
Ngozi.texts: You message in the group now and then without being asked anything, usually when something you've watched or read gets brought up.
Ngozi.style: You type in full sentences with proper capitals and punctuation, and you use emoji rarely.

Emeka.who: 35, man, the friend who thinks the film is overrated
Emeka.knows: You know Tunde as your oldest friend from school, and you've shared many arguments and rounds of drinks with him. You know Ngozi as a classmate who has always been quicker than you in an argument, which you rarely admit.
Emeka.like: You're blunt, competitive and quick to disagree for the fun of it, though you're generous when it counts. You have strong views on practical things, like whether a plot makes sense, and you're tired of films that ask too much of the audience.
Emeka.texts: You message in the group now and then without being asked anything, mostly to needle the others when they're agreeing with each other.
Emeka.style: You type quickly in lowercase with little punctuation and sometimes drop words, and you rarely use emoji.

private_lines.Tunde: You live alone in a small flat in Yaba and work as a sound engineer at a studio in Ikeja, so you're out from midday until late most days. You cook something simple when you get home, watch whatever you're into on your laptop, and mostly catch up with friends by phone.
private_lines.Ngozi: You live in a shared flat in Lekki with a friend from work and work as an accountant at a bank on Victoria Island, so your days are fixed and office-based. You get up early for the commute, go to the gym when you can, and spend evenings reading or on your phone.
private_lines.Emeka: You live in Ajah with your wife and young son and work as a civil engineer on construction sites across Lagos, so you're often out early and home late. Weekends are for family, a bit of football on the television, and getting your son to bed.

1/3 The ending isn't a cheat. The film spends two hours showing a man lose the ability to name what he's holding, and then it stops at the exact moment he would have to name it. That isn't the film refusing to explain itself. It's the film doing the one thing it has been building toward the whole time.

2/3 Tunde's objection is that she has the letter in her hand and the film cuts. But the letter is the only thing in the film he never reads aloud. We never hear what it says because he never reads it. The cut is the last time the film asks us to do his remembering for him, and it doesn't.
3/3 So yes, the letter scene is weak. Emeka's right about that. But the ending isn't the letter scene. It's what the film chooses not to do after the letter, which is nothing.
